hook: Release builds shrink your wasm binary dramatically.
body_md: wasm-pack builds debug output by default which is large and slow. Pass --release and tune the release profile with lto, codegen-units 1, and debug off. Compare file sizes in pkg before and after to see the win.
code:
[profile.release]
opt-level = "z"
lto = true
codegen-units = 1
debug = false
strip = true
takeaway: Release profiles trade slower builds for much smaller and faster wasm output.
trap: Shipping a debug build to production because --release was forgotten.

quiz.q: Which profile option helps shrink a release wasm binary?
quiz.explain: Size opts plus link-time optimization remove dead code and inline aggressively.

hook: One crate ships to web, bundler, and Node with targets.
body_md: wasm-pack --target selects the JS glue style: bundler for webpack or Vite, web for bare ES modules, nodejs for Node, no-modules for plain script tags. Pick the one matching your host, since imports and init differ per target.
code:
wasm-pack build --target bundler
wasm-pack build --target web
wasm-pack build --target nodejs
wasm-pack build --target no-modules
takeaway: Each wasm-pack target emits glue code shaped for a different module host.
trap: Using bundler glue with a plain script tag, which fails on bare imports.

quiz.q: Which target suits a plain script tag with no bundler?
quiz.explain: no-modules exposes a global instead of ES imports so script tags work.

hook: wasm-opt squeezes binaries after Rust is done.
body_md: Binaryen wasm-opt runs extra passes like dead-code elimination and inlining on the final wasm. Levels range from -O0 to -O4, with -Oz favoring size and -Os balancing size and speed. wasm-pack runs it automatically on release builds.
code:
wasm-opt -Oz input.wasm -o output.wasm
wasm-opt -O4 input.wasm -o fast.wasm
ls -lh input.wasm output.wasm
takeaway: Post-build optimization passes shrink wasm beyond what the compiler alone achieves.
trap: Running -O0 expecting shrinkage when only -O2 and above optimize hard.

quiz.q: What does -Oz prioritize over -O4?
quiz.explain: -Oz tunes passes for size while -O4 chases runtime speed.

hook: wasm-snip cuts functions you never call.
body_md: wasm-snip removes annotated or regex-matched functions from the binary, handy for stripping panics, formatting, or test helpers. Mark cold paths with Snip or pass a pattern. Always re-run tests after snipping to catch overreach.
code:
wasm-snip input.wasm -o slim.wasm \
  -p "__wbindgen.*"
ls -lh input.wasm slim.wasm
takeaway: Snipping deletes matched functions to reclaim space from unused helpers.
trap: Snipping a function that is actually reached through dynamic dispatch.

quiz.q: When is wasm-snip most useful?
options: Removing known-dead helpers to save bytes
quiz.explain: It pattern-deletes kept-but-unused functions the optimizer cannot prove dead.

hook: twiggy shows exactly what bloats your binary.
body_md: twiggy top lists the largest size contributors like monomorphized generics, panic machinery, or embedded formatting tables. Run it on release output, then attack the top rows by trimming features, sharing generics, or swapping allocators.
code:
twiggy top pkg/app_bg.wasm
twiggy top -n 20 pkg/app_bg.wasm
takeaway: Size profiling points the optimizer at the heaviest symbols first.
trap: Guessing at bloat instead of measuring and tuning the wrong crate.

quiz.q: What does twiggy top report?
options: Largest size contributors in the binary
quiz.explain: It ranks symbols and sections by bytes so you fix real bloat.

hook: Default allocator is heavy, tiny ones save kilobytes.
body_md: Rust binaries link a full allocator by default. wee_alloc and lol_alloc are tiny bump-style allocators that cut tens of kilobytes for small apps. They are slower under churn, so keep the system allocator for allocation-heavy workloads.
takeaway: Tiny allocators trade allocation speed for a much smaller binary footprint.
trap: Switching allocators in a hot loop app and wondering why it slowed down.

quiz.q: When does wee_alloc make sense?
options: Small apps where binary size matters most
quiz.explain: Its bump design is tiny but slower under allocation churn.

hook: Trunk builds apps while wasm-pack builds libraries.
body_md: Trunk watches index.html, compiles the crate, bundles CSS and assets, and serves with live reload, ideal for Leptos or Yew apps. wasm-pack produces an npm-style package for embedding in an existing site. Choose by whether Rust owns the page.
code:
trunk serve
trunk build --release
wasm-pack build --target web
takeaway: Trunk owns the whole page pipeline while wasm-pack ships a reusable package.
trap: Running wasm-pack for a full app and hand-wiring HTML the tool would manage.

quiz.q: You own a full Leptos page with assets, which tool fits?
quiz.explain: Trunk handles HTML assets and serving while wasm-pack targets libraries.

hook: Vite loads Rust wasm with two plugins.
body_md: Install vite-plugin-wasm plus vite-plugin-top-level-await, then import the pkg output in JS. Vite serves wasm with correct MIME types in dev and hashes it into dist on build. Restart dev after adding the plugins.
takeaway: Vite needs dedicated plugins to fetch and initialize wasm modules cleanly.
trap: Forgetting top-level-await plugin so init promises never resolve in dev.

quiz.q: Why add vite-plugin-top-level-await?
options: Wasm init uses top-level await in glue code
quiz.explain: The generated init runs at module top level, so the bundler must allow awaiting there.

hook: Webpack needs one flag to speak wasm.
body_md: Set experiments asyncWebAssembly true, then import the wasm like any module. Webpack fetches it asynchronously at runtime and splits it into its own chunk. Without the flag the build errors on the binary import.
takeaway: Enabling async wasm lets webpack chunk and load the binary at runtime.
trap: Importing wasm with experiments off and blaming Rust for the build error.

quiz.q: What breaks if asyncWebAssembly is missing?
options: The build fails on wasm imports
quiz.explain: Webpack only parses wasm modules when the experiment flag is on.

hook: Source maps connect panics back to Rust lines.
body_md: Build with debug info kept aside, then load the map in devtools so stack frames show Rust files instead of wasm offsets. Never ship full maps publicly; upload them to your error tracker or serve them locally only.
code:
wasm-pack build --dev
# keep maps local, strip for prod
wasm-pack build --release
takeaway: Debug maps translate raw wasm offsets into readable Rust source lines.
trap: Shipping full source maps publicly and leaking internal source paths.

quiz.q: Where should full wasm source maps live?
options: Local dev or a private error tracker
quiz.explain: They aid debugging but can expose sources if published openly.

hook: Devtools can breakpoint Rust through DWARF data.
body_md: Chrome and Firefox read embedded DWARF to show Rust sources in the debugger. Build with debug info, open Sources, find the original file, and step as usual. Variables may show optimized-out under release opts.
takeaway: Embedded debug data lets browsers step through original Rust sources directly.
trap: Debugging a stripped release binary and seeing only raw offsets.

quiz.q: What enables Rust-level breakpoints in the browser?
options: DWARF debug data in the build
quiz.explain: Devtools map wasm addresses to source lines using DWARF records.

hook: Memory Inspector reads raw linear memory bytes.
body_md: Open Chrome devtools Memory Inspector on a WebAssembly.Memory object to watch bytes change live. Point it at the buffer after instantiating, then write from Rust and see cells update. Great for debugging string or pixel encoding bugs.
takeaway: Live byte views reveal exactly what Rust wrote into shared memory.
trap: Holding a stale Uint8Array after memory grows and reading garbage.

quiz.q: What does Memory Inspector show?
quiz.explain: It renders the buffer so encoding bugs become visible immediately.

hook: Firefox shows WAT beside the running module.
body_md: In Firefox debugger, open the wasm source to see disassembled WAT with functions and locals. Set breakpoints on WAT instructions when Rust sources are missing. Copy function names from there into bug reports for precision.
code:
(module
  (func (export "add")
    (param i32 i32) (result i32)
    local.get 0
    local.get 1
    i32.add))
takeaway: Disassembled text views make stepping possible even without original sources.
trap: Assuming minified names match Rust names when reading raw disassembly.

quiz.q: When does the Firefox WAT view help most?
quiz.explain: WAT exposes real instructions and locals when source maps are absent.

hook: Safari runs wasm but lags on newest features.
body_md: WebKit supports core wasm plus threads and SIMD behind recent versions, so test on real iPhones not just desktop. Feature-detect WebAssembly and SIMD before using them, and keep a single-threaded fallback path for older releases.
takeaway: Guarded feature checks keep Apple devices on a working execution path.
trap: Assuming desktop Chrome behavior matches an old iPhone WebView.

quiz.q: What is the safest Safari strategy?
quiz.explain: Detection routes old WebKit to fallback instead of crashing on init.

hook: Node loads wasm with plain async instantiate.
body_md: Read the file into bytes, call WebAssembly.instantiate with an imports object, then call exports. No bundler needed. Keep the glue JS next to the binary and pin versions so server deploys stay reproducible.
takeaway: Server-side instantiation needs only file bytes plus an imports object.
trap: Passing a path string instead of bytes to instantiate.

quiz.q: What must you pass to WebAssembly.instantiate in Node?
quiz.explain: It compiles from bytes, so read the file first then instantiate.

hook: Deno runs wasm with zero installs.
body_md: Use Deno.readFile for bytes and WebAssembly.instantiate, same as browsers, with permissions guarding file access. Remote imports need --allow-net while local files need --allow-read. Cache the compiled module to skip recompiling each run.
takeaway: Deno permission flags wrap the same standard instantiation flow securely.
trap: Forgetting allow-read so local wasm loads fail with permission errors.

quiz.q: Which flag lets Deno read a local wasm file?
quiz.explain: File access is gated, so local bytes need explicit read permission.

hook: Bun starts wasm fast from its own file API.
body_md: Bun.file gives bytes quickly, then standard instantiate runs the module. Hot paths benefit from Bun fast startup, making it nice for CLIs and tests. Reuse one instance across calls instead of re-instantiating per request.
takeaway: Bun file helpers feed the standard loader with minimal startup overhead.
trap: Re-instantiating per request instead of reusing one warm instance.

quiz.q: What feeds WebAssembly.instantiate under Bun?
quiz.explain: The loader still consumes bytes, Bun just supplies them quickly.

hook: wasm-pack test runs Rust tests in real browsers.
body_md: Write #[wasm_bindgen_test] cases, then run wasm-pack test --headless --chrome or --firefox. It builds the crate, drives a headless browser, and reports failures like cargo test. Use it for DOM and fetch code that cannot run natively.
code:
wasm-pack test --headless --chrome
wasm-pack test --headless --firefox
takeaway: Headless browser harnesses exercise wasm code paths that native tests cannot reach.
trap: Only running native cargo test for DOM code that needs a browser.

quiz.q: What does wasm-pack test add over cargo test?
options: A real browser runtime for DOM cases
quiz.explain: It executes tests inside Chrome or Firefox where web APIs exist.

hook: cargo-bloat finds the generics eating your budget.
body_md: Run cargo bloat in release for the wasm target to rank crates and symbols by size. Generics, regex tables, and panic formatting usually top the list. Trim features, box large variants, or swap crates based on the ranking.
code:
cargo bloat --release --target wasm32-unknown-unknown
cargo bloat --release --crates
takeaway: Crate-level size ranking turns vague bloat into concrete removal targets.
trap: Removing random deps without measuring which one dominates size.

quiz.q: What guides diet decisions after cargo bloat?
options: The ranked size table of crates
quiz.explain: Largest rows give the best byte-per-effort savings first.

hook: A size checklist keeps bundles under budget.
body_md: Combine release profile, wasm-opt -Oz, stripped symbols, tiny allocator, and trimmed features. Measure with twiggy after each change and gate CI on a kilobyte limit. One knob rarely suffices; the stack compounds.
code:
[profile.release]
strip = true
# plus: wasm-opt -Oz, tiny alloc
# plus: default-features = false
takeaway: Layered size tactics compound into savings no single flag can match.
trap: Applying -Oz but shipping debug symbols that dwarf the savings.

quiz.q: Why layer several size tactics?
quiz.explain: Compiler, linker, allocator, and post passes each remove different waste.
